answers.question: What does a short, repeated exposure of a minute or two do to the body, and what does daily repetition add up to?
answers.bestAnswer: Nobody has shown that one red light makes you ill, but in Taiwan the body has been measured reacting within five minutes to small rises in fine dust (a small, temporary dip in heart-rate steadiness, about 1-2.5% per 10 ug/m3), the clearest harm in experiments appears after 1-2 hours in traffic, and a few red lights a day add up to roughly 12-55 hours a year.
answers.bestAnswerZh: 沒有人證明過等一個紅燈就會生病；但在台灣已經量到，細懸浮微粒只要在五分鐘內升高一點，心跳的穩定度就會立刻小幅、暫時地下降（每多10微克約降0.9至2.5%），實驗裡明確的傷害要在交通中待一至兩小時才看得到，而每天等幾次紅燈，一年累積起來大約是12至55小時。
answers.basis: Shortest measured effect: Lung et al. 2025 wore PM sensors and heart-rate-variability sensors on 55 people in Kaohsiung (2019-2020) and 50 in Bandung; 5-minute PM2.5/PM1 exposure had statistically significant immediate effects on HRV and heart rate in all Taiwanese subjects; HRV change for a 10 ug/m3 increase ranged -0.9% to -2.5% (not for LF/HF ratio). Dominant sources there were incense, factories, agricultural burning, so it is not scooter-specific. Controlled and field experiments with clear effects use 1-2 hours: 1 h cycling in Ottawa traffic (UFP IQR 18,200/cm3 lowered HF by 140 msec2 at 2 h and 224 at 4 h); 2 h walking on Oxford Street (FEV1 down up to 6.1% in asthmatics); German diary study: time in traffic within the previous hour OR 2.92 for heart attack (association, mostly car travel). Peak share: Goel & Kumar 2015 (Guildford): about 2% of commuting time at junction delays gave about 25% of respiratory dose in one run. Arithmetic for accumulation (assumption: 60-90 s wait per red light; 2, 4 or 6 red lights a day; the wait length is a reader assumption, Taipei summer reductions of 21-30 s and Taichung cycle cuts of 180->150 s in news reports show reds of the order of one to two minutes): 2 lights = 2-3 min/day = 12-18 h/yr; 4 lights = 4-6 min/day = 24-36 h/yr; 6 lights = 6-9 min/day = 36-55 h/yr (x365). These are minutes of exposure, not minutes of high concentration.
sources: Lung S-C C, et al. 2025. Peaks, sources, and immediate health impacts of PM2.5 and PM1 exposure in Indonesia and Taiwan with microsensors. J Expo Sci Environ Epidemiol. doi:10.1038/s41370-024-00689-4 (PMID 38806636). Opened abstract via Europe PMC; found figures. [verified]

answers.question: What health effects can be attributed to scooter exhaust specifically in Taiwan?
answers.bestAnswer: No Taiwanese study separates scooter exhaust from other traffic, but the closest answer is a 2022 Taiwanese roadside study beside a scooter-dominated road, which traced 57% of the lung-reaching particle surface (74% at rush hour, when 83% of vehicles were scooters) to traffic and estimated about 16 extra cancers per 100,000 people over a lifetime from that traffic exhaust.
answers.bestAnswerZh: 沒有任何台灣研究能把機車廢氣和其他交通分開；最接近的答案是2022年在北台灣機車為主的路邊所做的研究：進入肺部的微粒表面積有57%來自交通（尖峰時段機車占83%時達74%），並估算這種交通廢氣一輩子下來，每十萬人約多16人罹癌。
answers.basis: Chang et al. 2022 (J Hazard Mater 427:128188): roadside station in northern Taiwan; PMF + regression attributed 57% of LDSA to traffic overall; at rush hour the motorcycle fraction rose to 0.83, LDSA 77.6 +/- 9.9 um2/cm3, PNC 14,000 +/- 2,400/cm3, traffic share 74%; excess lifetime cancer risk from traffic 1.56e-4 = 15.6 per 100,000. Opened abstract via Europe PMC. This is a risk calculation using LDSA and assumed unit risk and exposure duration (full text not opened), and 'traffic' includes all vehicles, so it is an upper-bound-type indication for scooter-heavy streets, not a scooter-only attributable number. Supporting Taiwan evidence on scooters: Chuang 2020 (scooter commuters, PM2.5 53.6 vs subway 21.7 ug/m3, small BP/HR/8-OHdG rises per PM2.5). What Taiwan cohorts show about gasoline traffic: Pan et al. 2021 (12,098 adults, REVEAL-HBV, 22.9 y follow-up): per log-unit vehicle count trucks HR 1.24 (1.03-1.51) for CVD death, small cars HR 1.10 (0.94-1.27, not significant), total HR 1.13 (0.96-1.33); scooters were counted as a gasoline source but not reported separately. Source shares (TEDS 13.0, 2023, repo digest): motorcycles are 15.6% of CO and 10.0% of hydrocarbon emissions but only 1.3% of primary PM2.5 and 2.2% of NOx, so PM2.5-based health figures should not be assigned to scooters. Not found despite searching Europe PMC, NTU/NCL repositories: any Taiwanese cohort using motorcycle counts as the exposure.

answers.question: How much more does a child or a baby in a pushchair breathe at 0.6-1.0 m than an adult at 1.5 m?
answers.bestAnswer: Measured abroad, air at pushchair or child height typically holds about 10% more traffic particles than at adult height (from 5% lower to 59% higher depending on the study), and because children breathe 1.5 to 2 times more air for their body weight, a child at a kerb takes in roughly 1.7 to 2.2 times the adult dose per kilogram.
answers.bestAnswerZh: 國外實測顯示，嬰兒車或兒童高度的空氣，交通微粒通常比大人高度多約10%（各研究從低5%到高59%不等）；而且孩子每公斤體重吸進的空氣是大人的1.5至2倍，所以站在路邊的孩子，每公斤體重吸入的量大約是大人的1.7至2.2倍。
answers.basis: Height effect (not Taiwan; cars/diesel mainly): study-by-study series already on site: Morgantown +59% (PM2.5), Guildford pram up to +44% (fine particles), Mainz over +20% on 6 of 8 days (1.0 vs 1.6 m), Barcelona about +10% (UFP, 0.55 vs 1.70 m), Edinburgh NO2 5-15%, Guildford 2017 afternoon about +10% and morning about -5%, one Edinburgh PM2.5 study no consistent difference. These cannot be averaged, so 'about 10%' is the middle of the cluster, not a mean. A Tokyo roadside study reportedly found particles <0.5 um at 0.5 m about 2.9x those at 2.0 m (Nakashima et al., Aerosol Air Qual Res 2014) but NOx showed no height dependence; I could only see this in a search-tool summary (publisher page 403), so it is not used in the headline. Breathing: US EPA Exposure Factors Handbook 2011 Table 6-7 (per kg body weight, males): 0.5 to <1 y 0.48 m3/kg-day; 2 to <5 y 0.44; 5 to <7 y 0.42; 7 to <11 y 0.37; 30 to <40 y 0.24 (females 0.24 at 30-40). Ratios to adult 0.24: infant 2.0, age 2-5 1.8, age 5-7 1.75, age 7-11 1.5. Combined arithmetic: 1.10 x 1.5 = 1.7 (school-age); 1.10 x 2.0 = 2.2 (baby). Using the extremes of the height range: 0.95 x 1.5 = 1.4 to 1.59 x 2.0 = 3.2. The per-kg ratio is for daily average breathing, and children and adults breathe about the same absolute volume per minute when sedentary (EPA Table 6-2 light activity 6-<11 y 0.011 vs 21-<31 y 0.012 m3/min), so the extra is per kilogram of body, not per breath. Taiwan scooter tailpipes: no height measurement found.

answers.question: What are children exposed to riding pillion or walking to school?
answers.bestAnswer: Nobody has measured it in Taiwan, but in other scooter cities (Ho Chi Minh City, Bandung) children's own sensors show the scooter or motorbike ride to school is the highest-exposure part of a child's trip, and in Taipei adults on scooters breathed about 2.5 times the fine dust of people on the MRT (53.6 vs 21.7 micrograms per cubic metre), so a child on the back seat should be assumed to breathe what the rider breathes.
answers.bestAnswerZh: 台灣還沒有人量過；但在胡志明市、萬隆等同樣機車很多的城市，孩子自己背的感測器顯示，騎機車上學那一段是整趟路中暴露最高的；在台北，騎機車的成人吸到的細懸浮微粒約是搭捷運的2.5倍（每立方公尺53.6對21.7微克），所以坐在後座的孩子，可以當作吸到的和騎士差不多。
answers.basis: Direct child measurements in motorbike cities: (1) Ho Chi Minh City, 64 children aged 11-12, AirBeam3 personal PM2.5, Dec 2022-Jan 2023: median 25 ug/m3 overall; peaks at 06:00-07:00 and 18:00-20:30; microenvironments with highest median 36.7-71.1 ug/m3 included commuting by motorbike; road commuting raised exposure 21.1%; 'motorbike commuting resulted in higher PM2.5 levels than walking or cycling'. (2) Bandung and Kathmandu, 61 children aged 6-13, PurpleAir, 2023: mean personal PM2.5 48.0 and 45.8 ug/m3; commuting-microenvironment means 46.7 and 49.0 ug/m3 (Table 4; city order as printed); 'travelling by scooter/motorbike resulted in the highest mean PM2.5 concentration for all commuting methods'; mean scooter/motorbike and walking commute 13 min vs bus 49 min and car 52 min; school classroom lowest (41.2 and 33.7). Taiwan adult proxy: Chuang 2020, 120 adults, Taipei, 9-10 am: scooter 53.6 +/- 26.1, walking 42.7 +/- 22.6, subway 21.7 +/- 5.8 ug/m3; ratio scooter:subway 53.6/21.7 = 2.5. Taipei 2017 EPA commuter monitoring: motorcycle 32.1, bus 23.5, MRT 21.9, car 7.6 ug/m3. Child dose adds: breathing per kg is about 1.5 times an adult's at age 7-11 (EPA Table 6-7: 0.37 vs 0.24 m3/kg-day). Inference (not measured): a pillion child sits in the same traffic stream, and a helmet or mask changes little for fine particles. The 13 min mean commute and Taiwan trip times are other countries' data. Taiwan pillion share of school trips: no verified official figure found.
